subdivision.heading: Assessment of Costs by Assessment Officer

operative_text.controlling:
10.36(1)  After a judgment or order has been entered, an
assessment officer, in accordance with any Court direction or order,
may make an assessment of costs payable in accordance with rule
10.41 in any of the following circumstances:
(a) under rule 3.36(3);
(b) under rule 3.37;
(c) under rule 3.38;
(d) under rule 3.39.
(2)  In cases other than those referred to in subrule (1), the amount
assessed under rule 10.41 as payable by one party to another must
be determined by way of an appointment with an assessment
officer unless the Court or the assessment officer otherwise
permits.
(3)  Despite subrules (1) and (2), if one party approves a bill of
costs prepared by another party adverse in interest, an assessment
officer must certify the bill of costs under rule 10.43, without
change.

BOOK_A.title: Assessment of Bill of Costs
BOOK_A.operative_text_raw:
10.36(1) After a judgment or order has been entered, an assessment ofﬁcer, in
accordance with any Court direction or order, may make an assessment of costs
payable in accordance with rule 10.41 [Assessment officer’s decision] in any of
the following circumstances:
(a) under rule 3.36(3) [Judgment in default of defence and noting in
default];
(b) under rule 3.37 [Application for judgment against defendant noted in
default];
(c) under rule 3.38 [Judgment for recovery of property];
(d) under rule 3.39 [Judgment for debt or liquidated demand].
(2) In cases other than those referred to in subrule (1), the amount assessed
under rule 10.41 [Assessment officer’s decision] as payable by one party to
another must be determined by way of an appointment with an assessment
ofﬁcer unless the Court or the assessment ofﬁcer otherwise permits.
(3) Despite subrules (1) and (2), if one party approves a bill of costs prepared by
another party adverse in interest, an assessment ofﬁcer must certify the bill of
costs under rule 10.43 [Certification of costs payable], without change.⁵
BOOK_A.commentary:
See also the Rules set out in Schedule C.
August 2021 to January 2022 Court of King's Bench notices having a bearing on reviews and
assessments, and where to ﬁnd them, are described in R.10.13 n.
Rule 10.36(3) was applied even though not all the parties had consented, in a foreclosure
where it was proved that no one had a ﬁnancial interest or any real likelihood of being affected by
the costs other than the party which had consented.¹
A tariff of fees and an agreement with the sheriffs’ ofﬁce regulate the fees and expenses which
can be charged by civil enforcement agencies to enforce a money judgment. It is implicit that this
system gives ﬁgures which are reasonable and proper. The assessment ofﬁcer has no power to
vary them.²
Where a mortgage and a consent order call for solicitor-client costs, the assessment ofﬁcer
cannot cut them in half, even if there was and remains a costs guideline by the Masters.³
Where an executor or trustee has had years to document expenses incurred, and more time
will not produce more vouchers, proportional responses should be followed, given the duty of the
executor or trustee. Some expenses may be found legitimate without a voucher, and others may
be found not justiﬁed, and the fees of the executor or trustee may be reduced.⁴

footnotes.text: Quite similar to previous R.629.1. It was ﬁrst enacted as R.652.1, then moved to show that it applied to all bills of costs. The Alberta assessment ofﬁcers used to rely on Crédit Foncier Tr. Co. v. Hornigold (1984) 59 AR 103, 35 Alta LR(2d) 341, and would assess an account even when it was approved by counsel, unless the order speciﬁcally allowed counsel to agree on the costs. The 1992 amendment adding R.652.1 (now R. 629.1) reversed that interpretation. Then the Rule was relocated after R.629, by Alta. Reg.160/93.
Alta. Treas. Br. v.1401057 Alta.2013 ABQB 748, 579 AR 152.
Re Vanmaele Est.2019 ABCA 499, Edm 1803 0305 AC (Dec 17) (¶’s 27-29).

BOOK_B.title: Assessment of bill of costs

commentary.text: Rule 10.36 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.36. In Equitable Bank v. Avison, 2015 ABQB 109, 2015 CarswellAlta 222 (Master), Master Schulz emphasized the need for evidence in relation to assessments. The learned Master said, at paragraphs 30–35: 30 This matter went to the assessment officer at first instance. Counsel sent correspondence to the assessment officer in reference to a reduction in the fees claimed on the Bill of Costs wherein he stated that the assessment officer has … no authority to make this determination … The Defendant, Kenneth Avison, has no issue with regard to our Bill of Costs as there is a shortfall to the second mortgagee. As far as I know, the second mortgagee does not take issue with our Bill of Costs as the steps we took have been very beneficial to the second mortgagee. I am copying this letter to the second mortgagee through his solicitor. 31 It appears that this comment is made in reference to Rule 10.36(3): (3) Despite subrules (1) and (2), if one party approves a bill of costs prepared by another party adverse in interest, an assessment officer must certify the bill of costs under rule 10.43[Certification of costs payable]without change. [Emphasis added] 32 The Bill of Costs submitted to the assessment officer is not endorsed with the approval of the Defendant and there is no affidavit evidence of consent. Accordingly, Rule 10.36(3) does not apply. The assessment officer has the authority to assess the reasonableness of solicitor fees and disbursements. 33 Counsel is also reminded that the Court, and through it the assessment officers, have … an overriding obligation to ensure that those who are obliged to pay for legal services are treated reasonably, taking into account all the circumstances. This is an important function is all cases but particularly so when the person who may be liable to pay a lawyers' charges does not select the lawyer,” as here. Paradigm Quest Inc v Moser, 2014 ABQB 747 at para 12 (Schlosser, M.) (“Paradigm”), summarizing the tenth cost principle enunciated by Wakeling, J. (now J.A.) in Alberta Treasury Branches v 14010507 Alberta Ltd (Katch 22), 2013 ABQB 748 (“ATB”) 34 In correspondence to the assessment officer, Counsel indicates that the “fees set out in the Bill of Costs and Affidavit of Disbursement of Sale Proceeds are the actual legal costs recorded and billed”. The assessment officer is entitled to have evidence of this when assessing the reasonableness of the fees and disbursements and when applying the ten costs principles enunciated in the ATB case. As recommended by Master Schlosser at paragraph 32 of the Paradigm decision, Counsel would be well advised to produce the retainer agreement, evidence of the actual solicitor/client bill rendered to the client, the time dockets substantiating the charges, confirmation that the client has paid the account or at least approved it, and so on. It is up to Counsel to prove to the assessment officer that these are indeed the fees and disbursements charged to the client and that the client has agreed to be liable for that amount. In other words, the client has not imposed a tariff or cap to the fees and disbursements the lawyer can bill, in excess of which the client will not pay. 35 Similarly, Counsel would be well advised to provide copies of the invoices claimed as disbursements, preferably in affidavit form if requested by the assessment officer, keeping in mind that a review of the decision of the assessment officer is an appeal under Rule 10.26 to a justice and is on the record.
